newsitem.title: MEXICO: Amnesty faults Mexican army on human rights.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty faults Mexican army on human rights.

text.p: Amnesty International on Tuesday accused Mexico's security forces of unleashing a wave of human rights abuses as they cracked down on leftist rebels.

"We're in the country to document a theme that worries us extremely, the growing militarization of public force in Mexico," said Morris Tidball, an investigator at the London-based human rights watchdog.
"Hand in hand with that is the absolute impermeability of the armed forces to scrutiny, investigation and punishment of human rights violations," he said.

There was no official reaction from the Mexican government, but President Ernesto Zedillo met members of the government Human Rights Commission and urged them to work harder to make Mexico a country of law and order.

Zedillo "expressed his confidence that the...Commission will continue to contribute to consolidating a culture of respect for human rights and urged (the members) to help create a law-abiding culture," Zedillo's office said.

Tidball alleged that in the last two years death squads have emerged in Mexico, made up of paramilitary forces. He also said "forced disappearances," in which victims are picked up by the police and not seen again, have reached 30 in recent months.

Some of these, he said, were linked to efforts by the security forces to stop drug traffickers, but counter-insurgency has also taken its toll since the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) emerged in southern Mexico in June.

"Since the rise of the EPR, and the joint operations of the Attorney General's Office, the Mexican Army and Judicial Police forces in those states, an important number of social activists and journalists (have been victims)," he said.

He was speaking at a news conference unveiling a report on human rights workers in Mexico and Central America. The report alleged that threats, abduction and torture of these workers had soared in Mexico in the last four years.

Tidball said the current situation was alarmingly reminiscent of the 1970s, when a slew of rebel groups sprung up and military and paramilitary "white guard" units kidnapped, tortured and killed suspected leftists. He also likened the situation to the "dirty war" era of countries like Argentina.
In the report, Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo was portrayed as ineffectual in the fight against rights abuses.

"Since President Zedillo Ponce de Leon took office in December 1994, Amnesty International has documented more cases of threats against defenders of human rights than in any other era in three decades of investigating human rights violations in the country," it said.
Tidball said that Amnesty had launched more "urgent actions" this year in Mexico to denounce abuses than in any other country in the world. Many of these were in defence of human rights workers.
Mexico has usually come out cleaner than its Central American neighbours in documented cases of human rights abuses, but in the latest report it was just as tarnished.
